extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (and advanced high-school/olympiad) students learning introductory higher mathematics; readers of lecture-notes/napkin-style textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and structural conventions for writing/organizing introductory higher-mathematics lecture notes or a compact textbook: include precise definitions, prototypical examples, exercises, remarks, and motivating 'sales pitch' overviews for parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales pitch / part overview
rubrics_metrics.description: This chapter contains a pitch for each part, to help you decide what you want to read and to elaborate more on how they are interconnected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a short 'sales pitch' for each major part explaining what it covers, who it is for (algebraically inclined vs analytically inclined), how parts interconnect, and list a dependency plot so readers can choose reading order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prototypical example for each section
rubrics_metrics.description: Prototypical example for this section: [short descriptor such as 'The additive integers (Z,+)' or 'R^2 with the Euclidean metric'].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin sections by stating a single prototypical example that exemplifies the main idea of the section; repeat this pattern throughout (many sections begin with 'Prototypical example for this section: ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definitions followed by examples and non-examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition X.Y.Z. [formal definition]. Then provide multiple concrete examples and explicit non-examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the formal definition (e.g., group, metric space, open/closed set), then immediately follow with several worked examples, non-examples, and short exercises or questions that check comprehension (Example 1.1.1, Example 1.1.2, Example 1.1.6, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of remarks and pedantic points
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark X.Y.Z (Unimportant pedantic point) — Some authors like to add ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include short 'Remark' blocks to note pedantic conventions, subtle points, and alternative but equivalent formulations (e.g., closure axiom, notation choices). These remarks may be skippable for first-time readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of notation / notation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuse of Notation X.Y.Z. From now on, we’ll often refer to a group (G,⋆) by just G. Moreover, we’ll abbreviate a⋆b to just ab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly announce and justify convenient notational shortcuts (omitting parentheses for associative operations, switching between additive and multiplicative notation, using 0 vs 1 for identity in certain contexts) so readers know when conventions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured labeling: Definitions, Examples, Facts, Propositions, Lemmas, Theorems, Exercises, Questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions, Examples, Facts, Propositions, Lemmas, Theorems, Exercises, and Questions are used consistently to organize material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a consistent hierarchy and labels for mathematical objects and results; include short proofs or indicate when a proof is omitted; provide cross-references to appendices when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include exercises of varying difficulty and starred/hinted problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises and Problems (Problems 1A, 1B, 1C, Problem 1D⋆, Problem 1F†, etc.) are provided, with some marked as especially hard (⋆) or given hints (†).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide many exercises ranging from routine checks to challenging/olympiad-style problems; flag harder problems and sometimes provide hints or guidance; encourage readers to attempt proofs even when the main text omits details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate definitions with applications and intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivational paragraphs explaining why the topic matters (e.g., compactness makes real analysis 'tick'; determinant multiplicativity explained by linear maps; Shor's algorithm uses linear algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accompany formal definitions with motivating explanations, intuitive examples, and brief descriptions of significant applications to entice and orient readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide examples that illustrate 'why not' (non-examples and counterexamples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-Examples of groups: (Q,·) is NOT a group; (Z,·) is NOT a group; Mat2×2(R) with · is NOT a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly show common incorrect candidates and explain which axiom(s) fail, so readers internalize the necessity of each part of a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage visualization and pictures where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of a metric space is very 'concrete', and lends itself easily to visualization. Hence throughout this chapter you should draw lots of pictures as you learn about new objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For geometric or topological concepts, explicitly recommend drawing diagrams and geometric intuition (unit circle, disk, torus vs coffee cup, helix→circle covering example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include short proofs and indicate skippable formal manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs are shown briefly; others are noted 'you needn't feel bad skipping it on a first read'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide short formal proofs for key lemmas/facts; when proofs are routine, either sketch them or mark them as skippable while still stating the result for completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make constructive/robust choices explicit and show independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended example/definition: product metric — define several candidate metrics (dmax, dEuclid, dtaxicab) and show inequalities relating them so readers see the resulting topologies are homeomorphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple reasonable definitions exist, present alternatives and prove they are equivalent (or explain when they are not), to reassure readers that choices are not essential to core theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: State prototypical problems that illustrate typical proof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems such as 'Prove Lagrange’s theorem for orders in the special case that G is finite abelian' or 'Find subgroup H of S8 isomorphic to D8' are used to showcase key techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include representative problems that teach common techniques (pigeonhole, bijections, cancellation law, constructing isomorphisms) and that mirror the style of subsequent important proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thematic 'Questions' to prompt active engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Interspersed 'Question X.Y.Z' boxes check understanding (e.g., 'Why do we need p prime?' 'What are convergent sequences in a discrete metric space?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief conceptual questions to prompt the reader to test comprehension of definitions and examples immediately after exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide 'Examples of homeomorphisms' and counterpoints to naive expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples emphasizing that homeomorphism ≠ continuous bijection; show bounded vs unbounded spaces can be homeomorphic (e.g., (−1,1) ≅ R via tan/atan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confront intuitive misconceptions with explicit counterexamples and construct explicit homeomorphisms / continuous bijections with or without continuous inverses to illustrate distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State classical theorems with pointers to later proofs or generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem statements like 'Lagrange’s theorem for orders' are stated and readers are told to 'Keep this result in mind! We'll prove it later in the generality of Theorem 3.4.1.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce important results early in special cases to build intuition, and indicate where full proofs or generalizations will appear later, so readers can defer details without losing sight of the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly handle edge cases and technical definitions (open/closed sets, closures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of open and closed sets are given with multiple equivalent characterizations (neighborhood condition, pre-image condition, sequence characterization for closed sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For foundational notions, give all common equivalent formulations (ε-δ, neighborhood, sequence, complement) and prove equivalences; include exercises to cement the equivalences (e.g., open-set condition for continuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short 'digressions' and trivia to provide context and historical or heuristic notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Unimportant long digression and Trivia blocks give background such as why axioms were chosen or surprising facts (e.g., Cayley’s theorem remark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional digressions can motivate choices, provide historical context, or allay confusion; mark them as optional so they do not interrupt the main thread for readers who prefer concise development.
